$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$" :question/worked-solution "Using the usual formula, we get

$$
\frac{x-(-4)}{0}=\frac{y-5}{3}=\frac{z-1}{2}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

or equivalently

$$
\frac{x+4}{0}=\frac{y-5}{3}=\frac{z-1}{2},
$$

which is problematic because $\frac{x+4}{0}$ involves division by zero.

However, notice that in our line, the $x$ component always maintains the constant value of $x=-4:$

$$
r=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 5+3t \\ 1+2t\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

$$
\frac{y-5}{3}=\frac{z-1}{2},\,x=-4
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-1aa198ef-bba1-5d57-9850-a75e16ce7498"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨3,-1,1⟩-⟨-1,3,7⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-4,-6⟩.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$
\frac{x+1}{4}=\frac{y-3}{-4}=\frac{z-7}{-6}.

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{PQ} & =⟨3,-1,1⟩-⟨-1,3,7⟩ \\  & =⟨4,-4,-6⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the point $P$ and the vector $\overset{\to }{PQ}$, we have that the Cartesian (canonical) equation of the given line is given by

$$
\frac{x-(-1)}{4}=\frac{y-3}{-4}=\frac{z-7}{-6}=t,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ),
$$

$$
